title: Statism
summary: The political view that a person's life belongs to the state.

lessons.title: Name the view
lessons.objective: Identify statism as the political view that a person's life belongs to the state.

exercises.prompt: What does statism say about a person's life?

choices.text: It belongs to the state
It belongs only to that person
It belongs to no one at all
It belongs to whoever is luckiest

feedback.note: Statism is the political view that a person's life belongs to the state.

exercises.prompt: Match each name to the claim it makes.

pairs.right: A person's life belongs to the state
Not a political view about who owns a life
Not a claim about political ownership

feedback.note: Only statism, in this unit, is the view that the state owns a person's life. Everyday facts are not that view.

exercises.prompt: Complete the name of this unit's view.

parts.text: The view that a person's life belongs to the state is called

feedback.note: The name for that ownership claim is statism.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that states the view.

feedback.note: The whole claim is short: statism says a life belongs to the state.

exercises.prompt: Statism is which kind of view?

choices.text: A political view about who a life belongs to
A recipe for a meal
A map of rivers
A rule for rhyming songs

feedback.note: Statism is political. It answers who a person's life belongs to, and it answers: the state.

exercises.prompt: Match each phrase to the view it states.

pairs.left: Your life belongs to the state
Lives have no owner in politics

feedback.note: The distinctive line of statism assigns the life to the state. The other lines do not.

exercises.prompt: Fill in both sides of the claim.

feedback.note: What is owned is the person's life. Who owns it, on this view, is the state.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that keeps the name tied to politics.

feedback.note: Call it a political view, not a private taste or a craft rule.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is statism?

choices.text: A person's life belongs to the state
A person's life belongs to that person
A person's life belongs to the sky
A person's life is not a political topic

feedback.note: If the sentence gives the life to the state, it is stating statism.

exercises.prompt: A student says statism is only a nickname for any government. What is wrong with that?

choices.text: Statism names a specific claim: a life belongs to the state
Nothing is wrong; any government is statism
Statism names a kind of food
Statism names a favorite color

feedback.note: This unit uses statism for one political view, the view that a person's life belongs to the state.

lessons.title: Who the owner is
lessons.objective: Name the state, not the person, as the owner statism assigns to a life.

exercises.prompt: Under statism, who owns a person's life?

choices.text: The state
The person whose life it is
The person and the state as equal owners
No one

feedback.note: Statism picks one owner: the state. It does not leave the life with the person.

exercises.prompt: Match each answer to the question 'Who owns the life?'

feedback.note: The owner named by statism is the state, not the individual and not a noise contest.

exercises.prompt: Complete who holds the life on this view.

parts.text: Statism assigns ownership of the life to the

feedback.note: The contrast inside the claim is state versus person. The state is the owner.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that names the owner.

feedback.note: On this view the state is not a guest in the person's life. It is the owner.

exercises.prompt: A speaker says the person keeps title to his life and the state only borrows it. Is that statism?

choices.text: No. Statism says the life belongs to the state
Yes. Borrowing is the same as belonging
Yes, if the loan is written in the sky
Yes, because half ownership is full ownership

feedback.note: Belonging to the state is ownership by the state. A loan that leaves title with the person is a different claim.

exercises.prompt: Match each owner-word to what statism does with it.

pairs.right: Named as the owner of the life

feedback.note: Statism does not say the life is unowned. It moves ownership to the state.

exercises.prompt: Fill the owner statism names.

parts.text: The owner of the life, according to statism, is the

feedback.note: One word carries the ownership: state.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that rejects the person as owner.

feedback.note: Statism denies that the person is the owner of his own life.

exercises.prompt: Which pair matches statism?

choices.text: Life owned by the state
Life owned by the person
Life owned by no one
Life owned by the weather

feedback.note: The matching pair is the life and the state as its owner.

exercises.prompt: If two people disagree only about the flag's colors, are they disagreeing about statism's owner?

choices.text: No. Statism's owner question is who the life belongs to
Yes. Flag colors decide who owns a life
Only if the flag is large
Yes, every disagreement is about ownership

feedback.note: The owner question in this lesson is narrow: statism says the state, not the person.

lessons.title: What the life covers
lessons.objective: Treat the life that statism assigns to the state as including the person's work, time, and choices.

exercises.prompt: If a life belongs to the state, which of these does statism treat as the state's as well?

choices.text: The person's work, time, and choices
Only rocks that no one touches
Only dreams the person never acts on
Only the motion of the stars

feedback.note: A life, in this claim, is not an empty label. It covers the work, time, and choices that make the life.

exercises.prompt: Match each part of a life to how statism treats it.

pairs.right: Belongs to the state with the life
Belongs to the state with the life
Belongs to the state with the life
Not part of this ownership claim

feedback.note: Work, time, and choices travel with the life. Unrelated facts about planets do not.

exercises.prompt: Complete what rides along with the life.

feedback.note: Giving the state the life is giving it the work and the choices, not only a slogan.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence about time.

feedback.note: Time is part of the life statism assigns to the state.

exercises.prompt: Someone says the state owns the life but the person still owns every choice. What does this lesson say?

choices.text: That splits the claim. Choices are part of the life
That split is what statism means
Choices belong to the state only on weekends
Lives never include choices

feedback.note: If the life belongs to the state, the choices that are the living of it belong there too.

exercises.prompt: Match each item to whether statism's ownership claim covers it.

pairs.left: The color of a far star

feedback.note: The claim reaches the person's time and choices. It does not reach unrelated facts.

exercises.prompt: Fill the three parts this lesson includes.

feedback.note: Remember the trio that travels with the life: work, time, and choices.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence about work.

feedback.note: Work is not a side item. Under this claim it goes with the life to the state.

exercises.prompt: Which is outside the ownership claim in this lesson?

choices.text: The orbit of the moon
The person's choice of work
The person's hours
The tasks the person does

feedback.note: The moon's path is not the person's life. Work, hours, and tasks are.

exercises.prompt: Why does this lesson mention work, time, and choices together?

choices.text: They are what the owned life consists of
They are a random list of nouns
They describe the sky
They are things the claim leaves to the person

feedback.note: The point is scope. Belonging covers the living of the life, not a word with nothing in it.

lessons.title: The person as a means
lessons.objective: Explain that statism treats the person as a means to the state's ends because the life belongs to the state.

exercises.prompt: If the life belongs to the state, what is the person for, on this view?

choices.text: A means to the state's ends
The owner who sets every end
Someone with no connection to ends
A means only to the weather

feedback.note: An owned life is used for the owner's ends. Statism makes those ends the state's, so the person is a means.

exercises.prompt: Match each role to the view that assigns it.

pairs.left: Person as a means to the state's ends
Person as the owner of his life
State as a tool the person may ignore

feedback.note: Statism reverses the roles: the state holds the life, and the person serves the state's ends.

exercises.prompt: Complete the role statism gives the person.

parts.text: Statism treats the person as a

feedback.note: Means and ends stay paired: the person is the means, and the ends belong to the state.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that states the role.

feedback.note: Serving the state's ends is what it means to be a means once the life belongs to the state.

exercises.prompt: Why does the means follow from the ownership claim?

choices.text: What belongs to the state is there for the state's ends
Because a coin flip said so
Because means rhymes with state
It does not follow at all

feedback.note: Ownership is for use toward the owner's ends. That is why the person becomes a means.

exercises.prompt: Match each phrase to its place in the claim.

pairs.right: What the person is used for
Why the person is a means

feedback.note: Life owned by the state, person as the means, state's ends as the purpose: that is one chain.

exercises.prompt: Fill who is served.

parts.text: The person is a means, and the ends that are served are the

feedback.note: The ends in this view are the state's, not an empty or outside purpose.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that keeps ownership as the reason.

feedback.note: The means is not a separate slogan. It is what ownership by the state implies.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence stays inside this lesson?

choices.text: Because the life belongs to the state, the person is a means to its ends
A majority vote is always the same as a right
Prices are a kind of weather
A painting must copy every leaf

feedback.note: This lesson stays on one link: owned life, therefore the person is a means to the state's ends.

exercises.prompt: Can the person be the owner of the life and merely a means to the state's ends at the same time, on this unit's terms?

choices.text: No. The means role follows because the state, not the person, owns the life
Yes. Owner and means are the same role
Yes, but only on one day a week
Yes, if the person says the word means

feedback.note: Statism's means role depends on the state being the owner. It is not an extra title the person keeps while remaining the owner.

lessons.title: Spot the wording
lessons.objective: Recognize the same statism claim when it is worded as a duty to the state, a national purpose, or the public's ownership of the person.

exercises.prompt: Someone says each person owes his life as a duty to the state. Which view is that?

choices.text: Statism, in different words
A cooking tip
A claim about map colors
A denial that lives belong to anyone

feedback.note: A duty to hand one's life to the state is the same ownership claim under another wording.

exercises.prompt: Match each wording to the claim it makes.

pairs.left: Your life is a duty owed to the state
You exist for the national purpose

feedback.note: Duty, national purpose, and public ownership are three ways of saying the life belongs to the state.

exercises.prompt: Complete the hidden claim.

parts.text: A duty of one's life to the state still means the life belongs to the

feedback.note: Changing duty for belongs does not change the owner. The owner is still the state.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that equates the wordings.

feedback.note: Saying a person exists for a national purpose restates the view that the life belongs to the state.

exercises.prompt: The public owns you is closest to which line?

choices.text: A person's life belongs to the state
A person's life belongs to that person
No one has a life
The sky owns the tides only

feedback.note: Public ownership of the person is another wording of the state's ownership of the life.

exercises.prompt: Match each slogan to whether it is statism.

pairs.left: Hand your years to the nation

feedback.note: Purpose-of-the-state language and handing over years are the same claim. Keeping the life is not.

exercises.prompt: Fill two wordings that still mean statism.

parts.text: to the state and a national

feedback.note: Duty and national purpose are disguises of one view, not new views.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence about public ownership.

feedback.note: Calling the owner the public does not leave the claim. It is still statism.

exercises.prompt: Which wording is not statism?

choices.text: The person keeps his own life
Life is a duty owed to the state
The nation is the purpose of the person
The public owns the person

feedback.note: Keeping one's own life contradicts the claim. The other three wordings repeat it.

exercises.prompt: What should you do when the wording changes but the life is still assigned to the state?

choices.text: Count it as the same view, statism
Invent a new view for every synonym
Drop the topic because the verb changed
Treat it as a report about the sky

feedback.note: Duty, national purpose, and public ownership are statism when they still give the person's life to the state.
